links.targetTitle: ACs get an opportunity to respond but are explicitly denied

title: The Atlas admits it lacks fact-finding and evidence protocols while already mandating strict adjudication
content:
NR-1 ("Systematic Basis Of Adjudication, Fact-Finding And Evidence") is the Atlas assessing its own adjudication machinery. It grants that "the Atlas has made a good start with establishing an adjudication framework" and that there is "some logic concerning procedures for how disputes and controversies... are brought forward and how they are reviewed." Then: "But essential elements are missing, such as protocols and standards for fact-finding and evidence."

The open questions it lists are foundational, not marginal: "Who has the authority to investigate, to request evidence, to handle evidence? What types of evidence are permissible to consider, and what ethical considerations apply to how such evidence was obtained?... What criteria should be used to validate and evaluate evidence?" It also asks directly "how much discretion should Facilitators have in interpreting and applying the element 'the highest standard of Universal Alignment'" and how to "safeguard against bias."

The tension with A.1.5.4.0.4.1 is structural rather than verbal. That Tenet already imposes a quantified standard of proof — 51% — and makes derecognition mandatory once it is met, while explicitly barring lenience. A standard of proof presupposes a process for producing and weighing proof; NR-1 says that process does not yet exist. The framework has therefore fixed the threshold before fixing the measurement.

The Atlas is not hiding this, and the honest reading is that operational necessity outran procedural development: ACs hold power now, so a standard was needed now. NR-1's own proposed direction is telling about the priority ordering — it floats "independent review panels (which could operate post facto to avoid excessively delaying the deplatforming of misaligned ACs)." Even the remedy for missing due process is designed not to slow removal down.

Worth reading alongside NR-2 and NR-3, which similarly question whether the single-role rule in A.1.5.5 — ACs "may only be operationally active in a single AC role" — is drawn at the right boundary, given that "quality contributors are a scarce resource" and cross-team experience "might arguably enhance ecosystem intelligence." The Atlas ships its rules together with its doubts about them.
description: NR-1 concedes 'essential elements are missing' — who may investigate, what evidence is permissible, how it is evaluated — even though A.1.5.4 already compels derecognition on a 51% finding.
